# On the Peculiar Gift of Boredom

I've been thinking about boredom lately, and how we've declared war on it.

We carry glowing rectangles everywhere, designed by brilliant people whose explicit job is to make sure we're never unstimulated for more than three seconds. It's working spectacularly. The average person now experiences genuine, undirected boredom perhaps twice a year, usually when their phone dies.

But here's what I think we've lost: boredom is where ideas live.

Not productivity. Not the gamified, boxed-in "creative breakthroughs" that happen during designated brainstorm sessions. I mean the real stuff—the wandering thoughts that connect two unrelated things and suddenly something clicks. This happens in the shower, on long drives, or while staring out a window. It happens when your mind is free to be inefficient.

Our ancestors would have experienced *crushing* amounts of boredom—walking for hours, waiting for things, working repetitive tasks. Maybe they had the ideas that built civilization not despite the boredom, but because of it. Their brains had permission to wander.

I'm not suggesting we all abandon our devices and become monks. That's neither realistic nor desirable. But maybe the increasing sense that something's missing—that feeling a lot of people describe as a kind of low-level anxiety—isn't a bug in how we're living. Maybe it's a feature. Maybe we've become so afraid of boredom that we've forgotten it was never the enemy.

The enemy was never boredom itself. It was always just the inability to think.
